clips.title: 5 Claude Code Hooks That Save Me Hours Every Day
clips.why: A quick explanation of what a Claude Code hook is and how you add your first one, before we use a Stop hook to run verify.
look: A hook is a command that Claude Code runs by itself at a fixed moment.
Hooks are configured in a settings file, not in the prompt.
Which moment you pick decides what the hook can do.
clips.after: fcp's Stop hook uses exactly this: at the moment the agent wants to finish, it runs poe verify and answers with an exit code.

clips.title: Alex Shaw (Laude Institute): Using Harbor to run agent evals at scale.
clips.why: Alex Shaw, who builds Harbor, explains what an agent eval is and how a Harbor task is specified, the folder you write in the lab.
look: An eval gives the agent a task in an environment and then checks the result.
The parts of a task: the instruction, the environment, and the tests that decide the reward.
Why the same task format works for many different agents.
clips.after: TICKET-BENCH is a set of these tasks made from old fcp tickets, run with an adapter that starts Nova's real harness.

clips.title: Everything Is a Rollout — Alex Shaw + Ryan Marten, Terminal-Bench, Harbor, Laude Institute
clips.why: The same team on the different kinds of agent evaluations, so you can place a task with hidden tests among them.
look: The kinds of evaluation they separate.
Where a task that is checked by tests fits.
Why a fixed set of tasks lets you compare two versions of an agent.
clips.after: TICKET-BENCH is the test-checked kind: each task has hidden tests, and a harness change is compared on the same tasks.

practice.q: A Stop hook found red tests. Which exit code sends the agent back to work instead of ending the session?
practice.why: For a Stop hook, exit code 2 blocks the stop and shows the agent what the hook wrote to stderr.

practice.q: Why does verify lint and test only the files changed since the merge base, while CI runs verify --full?

options.text: Agents and people need a fast answer about their own change; CI can afford the full run and catches what the shortcut misses.
options.why: The affected run is quick enough to run at every stop. The full run is the safety net.

options.text: Linting unchanged files is not allowed in fcp.
options.why: It is allowed, just slower. --full does exactly that.

options.text: The merge base has no tests.
options.why: It has all of main's tests. The point is speed, not missing tests.

practice.q: Put the life of one bench task in order.
items: Harbor builds the task's environment from its Dockerfile
The agent reads instruction.md and works in the container
Harbor copies the hidden tests in and runs tests/test.sh
Harbor collects the rewards of all trials into the mean score
practice.why: The agent never sees the tests: they arrive only after it has finished, and the reward file is the only result Harbor reads.

practice.q: Prove that a new task cannot be passed by doing nothing.
practice.hint: The built-in agent that does nothing at all.
practice.why: The nop agent changes nothing, so a good task scores 0 with it. The oracle agent must score 1.

practice.q: Over three tries each, task A passes 3 of 3 and task B passes 1 of 3. What are the bench's pass@1 and pass^3?

options.why: pass@1 averages the success rates (1.0 and 0.33). pass^3 averages whether all three tries passed (1 and 0).
That swaps the two: the consistency score can never be higher than the single-try score.
That counts a task as passed if any try passed, which hides task B's two failures.
